missions.title: A second location
missions.scene: The operations manager says the current IT provider is fine, then mentions a new location opening in six weeks.

rounds.title: Catch the signal
rounds.quote: “We are all set. We just have a lot going on with the new office.”

options.text: The new office may change support needs. Ask how the opening is being handled.
options.why: You use a concrete plan the contact volunteered. A change can create a useful conversation even when the current provider is valued.

options.text: A new office proves their provider cannot keep up.
options.why: You turn a change into an unsupported problem. First find out how the work is covered.

options.text: Ask whether they are unhappy with IT.
options.why: You are trying to discover a need, but the question ignores the specific plan they just shared.

rounds.title: Follow the answer
rounds.quote: “Our IT lead is doing the setup and still handling everyone’s day-to-day requests.”

options.text: Would a lower monthly IT price help?
options.why: The SDR does not quote prices, and price was not the issue raised. Explore the workload and its effect.

options.text: How is that split affecting the setup timeline or everyday support?
options.why: You connect workload to a business outcome without assuming there is a failure.

options.text: How many computers do you have?
options.why: Size can help qualify an account, but it does not follow the workload signal yet.

rounds.title: Earn a fitting next step
rounds.quote: “We are concerned about the timeline. I could talk with someone about extra project capacity.”
rounds.prompt: How would you close this moment?

options.text: Offer a discovery conversation about the opening timeline and scope, confirm who should join, and agree a time.
options.why: The contact welcomed a specific discussion. Confirm purpose, participants and timing, then let the discovery team validate scope.

options.text: Promise that the MSP will finish everything before opening day.
options.why: Delivery dates require a scoped assessment by the responsible team. The SDR can arrange that discussion.

options.text: Email a brochure and leave the next step open.
options.why: A brochure may help, but you have a welcomed discovery opening. Make the next action explicit.

missions.title: “We have Microsoft 365”
missions.scene: A director says Microsoft 365 and two-step verification mean they already have everything covered.

rounds.title: Respect what is in place
rounds.quote: “We have Microsoft 365 and two-step verification, so we do not need an MSP.”

options.text: Explain that those tools are useless without your MSP.
options.why: That dismisses their investment and makes an unsupported technical claim.

options.text: Acknowledge the tools, then ask who handles user support, account changes and service coordination.
options.why: You respect the setup and explore the broader operating model. MSP conversations can include support, cloud and coordination as well as security.

options.text: List every service your MSP might offer.
options.why: The broader scope matters, but a service list creates little discovery. Start with how support is managed.

rounds.title: Use the business impact
rounds.quote: “Our office manager handles access changes. New hires sometimes wait until the afternoon.”

options.text: What does that delay mean for a new hire’s first day, and how often does it happen?
options.why: You explore impact and frequency before deciding whether onboarding support is relevant.

options.text: Recommend a particular technical configuration immediately.
options.why: Detailed technical design belongs in discovery with the appropriate specialist.

options.text: Ask whether they would like better IT.
options.why: It is a broad interest question. A question about the actual onboarding delay would produce better context.

rounds.title: Keep the promise honest
rounds.quote: “Could your team take responsibility for onboarding support?”
rounds.prompt: What can the SDR responsibly offer?

options.text: Guarantee zero waiting time for every new employee.
options.why: An absolute outcome is unsupported. Response commitments depend on the approved agreement and process.

options.text: Say it is probably possible, then move straight to a demo.
options.why: You avoid an absolute guarantee, but you still need a clear purpose and scope for the next discussion.

options.text: Connect the need to the approved support service and offer discovery to confirm responsibilities, process and coverage.
options.why: You position a relevant service and make confirmation part of a meaningful next step.

missions.title: The boss is on vacation
missions.scene: A gatekeeper says the decision-maker is away and offers to pass along an email.

rounds.title: Work with the route
rounds.quote: “My boss is on vacation. Send me something and I will pass it on.”

options.text: Ask for the boss’s personal mobile number.
options.why: A private number is not needed to use the offered route. Respect the contact’s role and boundaries.

options.text: Thank them and ask what topic would make the message useful to the boss.
options.why: You work with the offered route and try to make the message relevant.

options.text: Send a general brochure immediately.
options.why: You follow the requested channel, but a brief clarification could make the email more useful.

rounds.title: Separate permission from assumption
rounds.quote: “Include something about support coverage. She returns next Thursday.”

options.text: “Would a brief call the following week be useful, or would you prefer we leave the next move with her?”
options.why: You offer a proportionate choice. A return date is context, not automatic permission to schedule a callback.

options.text: Add a calendar meeting for Thursday without asking.
options.why: An absence date is not an accepted appointment.

options.text: Say that you will keep trying daily until she returns.
options.why: Repeated calls do not follow the offered route or a welcomed agreement.

rounds.title: Honor the answer
rounds.quote: “Please just send it. She will contact you if she wants to.”

options.text: Agree to the email, document the requested topic and that no callback was welcomed, then close politely.
options.why: You explored follow-up reasonably and accepted the answer. Record what was agreed without inventing a meeting or callback.

options.text: Ask for a callback one more time using different words.
options.why: The contact has clarified the boundary. Further pressure can damage the relationship.

options.text: Record “discovery meeting pending”.
options.why: An email route is not a discovery appointment. Accurate notes protect the next interaction.

missions.title: An active agreement
missions.scene: A prospect has a current MSP contract and says the relationship is working well.

rounds.title: Treat the contract as context
rounds.quote: “We have a contract through next year, and we are happy.”
rounds.prompt: What is reasonable if their tone remains receptive?

options.text: Ask whether there is a usual review window or any separately planned project where an introduction could be relevant.
options.why: You explore timing or a distinct need without implying they should break a contract.

options.text: Tell them a contract should not stop them from switching.
options.why: You dismiss their commitment instead of understanding the situation.

options.text: Assume every contract objection is a firm no-contact request.
options.why: You avoid pressure, but a receptive contact may still welcome one relevant clarification.

rounds.title: Recognize a closed opening
rounds.quote: “No projects to discuss. We are not reviewing alternatives and do not want follow-up.”

options.text: They need a stronger fear-based cybersecurity pitch.
options.why: The new information closes the discussion. Pressure does not create a viable opportunity.

options.text: The contact has declined further discussion and follow-up; end the pitch.
options.why: You use the actual answer to reassess viability. A good SDR recognizes when the available opening has ended.

options.text: Ask them to accept a meeting just to compare options.
options.why: That repeats the pitch after a clear boundary.

rounds.title: Choose a responsible disposition
rounds.quote: “Thank you. We really do not want more sales calls.”

options.text: Mark for recycle and call from another number next month.
options.why: Recycle creates no permission and cannot be used to evade a contact restriction.

options.text: Close politely, record the restriction accurately and follow the approved no-contact process.
options.why: This is a successful professional exit. Protect the relationship and apply the organization’s approved contact restriction process.

options.text: Stop calling but email weekly instead.
options.why: Changing channels to bypass a stated restriction is not a respectful next step.

missions.title: The internal IT team
missions.scene: A prospect values their internal team and asks about an outside assessment, while making clear they do not want co-management.

rounds.title: Understand the boundary
rounds.quote: “We have internal IT. We are not looking for co-management.”
rounds.prompt: How would you respond if they remain willing to talk?

options.text: Explain that their internal team cannot manage everything.
options.why: You assume a capability gap and risk making the conversation adversarial.

options.text: Acknowledge that preference and ask whether any independently scoped project or outside review is relevant.
options.why: You respect the model and explore only a distinct, potentially welcomed service.

options.text: Rename co-management as a partnership and pitch the same arrangement.
options.why: Changing the label does not respect the stated preference.

rounds.title: Clarify assessment interest
rounds.quote: “An outside review might help before our cloud project. Would that cost anything?”

options.text: Promise the assessment is free with no conditions.
options.why: Fees, scope and commitments must come from approved account terms.

options.text: Say assessments always lead to paid services.
options.why: That is also an unsupported claim. Use verified account-specific terms.

options.text: Explain the approved terms if confirmed; otherwise offer to confirm scope, eligibility, fees and obligations with the responsible team.
options.why: You handle the question honestly without inventing a price or condition.

rounds.title: Close on the actual purpose
rounds.quote: “Yes, let’s speak about a one-time review before the cloud project.”
rounds.criterion: Match the CTA to the welcomed service

options.text: A discussion about the review, project timing and participants, with the no-co-management preference recorded.
options.why: The discovery purpose matches the interest they expressed, and the handoff preserves an important boundary.

options.text: An opportunity to replace their entire IT team.
options.why: That contradicts the agreed purpose and could undermine trust during discovery.

options.text: An unconfirmed paid assessment order.
options.why: Interest in a discussion is not an order or acceptance of unconfirmed terms.

missions.title: Corporate makes the decision
missions.scene: The local contact says the old director has left and corporate controls IT purchasing.

rounds.title: Correct the contact record
rounds.quote: “That director no longer works here. Corporate handles IT now.”
rounds.prompt: What is the useful next move?

options.text: Ask for the former director’s personal contact details.
options.why: That does not help establish the current approved business route.

options.text: Thank them, confirm the current department or role, and ask how corporate accepts relevant vendor introductions.
options.why: You correct the record and work toward the right stakeholder without forcing a local decision.

options.text: Keep pitching the local contact as the decision-maker.
options.why: The contact has told you that the authority sits elsewhere.

rounds.title: Make a general inbox useful
rounds.quote: “We only give out the general IT inbox. Please include your purpose.”

options.text: Ask whether a specific subject line or department name helps route a support-services introduction.
options.why: A small routing detail can improve the message while respecting the limited access offered.

options.text: Insist on a direct email or refuse the general inbox.
options.why: You reject the route they are authorized to provide without evidence of another opening.

options.text: Invent the director’s email address.
options.why: Guessing a contact is not a verified route or an agreed next step.

rounds.title: Record progress accurately
rounds.quote: “Use ‘IT vendor introduction’. I cannot promise anyone will reply.”
rounds.prompt: How should you finish and document it?
rounds.criterion: Separate a route from a commitment

options.text: Record a corporate meeting booked because the email was accepted.
options.why: Acceptance of a message is not a meeting agreement.

options.text: Record the corrected role, approved inbox and subject, send the relevant message, and note that no response or callback was promised.
options.why: You made useful progress within the access available and left an accurate handoff.

options.text: Assume the gatekeeper agreed to personally sponsor the MSP.
options.why: The contact offered routing information, not sponsorship.
